title: Accelerated reliability testing of Cu-Al bimetallic contact by a micropattern corrosion testing platform for wire bond device application
author: Ashok Kumar, Alptekin, et al.

steps.title: Watch video and note changes
steps.instruction: Play the timelapse video in fast‑forward mode and record the timestamps of any notable surface alterations such as pitting, undercutting, surface oxidation, dendrite formation, and gas evolution.

steps.title: Determine event initiation times
steps.instruction: Using the recorded timestamps, calculate the time at which each event (e.g., first gas evolution) begins. Qualitatively relate these initiation times to the reactivity of the galvanic system and, if desired, verify the observation with an electroanalytical technique such as Zero Resistance Ammetry.

steps.title: Inspect morphology frame‑by‑frame
steps.instruction: Return to each noted timestamp and view the video one frame at a time, documenting detailed morphological changes, including the exact location where dendrite growth initiates and any accompanying phenomena such as gas evolution.

steps.title: Zoom for high‑resolution analysis
steps.instruction: Using high‑quality imaging, digitally zoom into individual frames to closely examine the boundary between the deposited metal dot and the substrate for finer morphological details.

steps.title: Validate microdot platform against real device
steps.instruction: Perform immersion screenings to confirm that the microdot corrosion platform reproduces the behavior of real wire‑bond devices.

substeps.instruction: Immerse the microdot pattern (Cu dot on blanket Al containing 0.5 % Cu) in a 5 ppm chloride solution at pH 5 for 2 h.
Immerse a real Cu wire‑bond device in a 20 ppm chloride solution at pH 5 for 1 h.
Compare the resulting corrosion morphology, noting dendrite formation extending from the Cu/Al interface and accompanying hydrogen gas evolution.
Confirm the evolved hydrogen gas by GC‑MS monitoring the m/z = 2 signal.

description: As seen in Figs. 2 and 3, the corrosion around the simulated and real bond pads follow the same general mechanism. There was a dendrite formation that extended from the Cu/Al interface and propagated through the bond pad. This was accompanied by hydrogen gas evolution (confirmed by GC-MS, in Fig. 4) [7]. Since the corrosion mechanism of the microdot platform replicates that of the real wire bond device in immersion screenings, the microdots can be used in place of real devices when exploring the use of different corrosion inhibitors and the effects of different contaminants within solution.Fig. 2A.
